multipeak-data.t: The same **16 customers' spend**. The values clump into **three groups**, so a good description of the data should have **three peaks**.

single-distribution-problem.t: A single bell curve fitted to this data sits at the mean, **4.92**, with standard deviation **2.34**. Its peak lands **between** the groups and it misses the clumps near 2 and 8.

component-a.t: We describe the **left clump** with its own bell curve: mean **2**, spread **0.8**, scaled down by its weight **0.30** because it covers only part of the data.

component-b.t: Component B covers the **middle clump**: mean **5**, spread **1.0**, weight **0.45**. It is the largest group, so it has the largest weight.

component-c.t: Component C covers the **right clump**: mean **8**, spread **0.9**, weight **0.25**. Each component is a simple bell curve responsible for one region.

mixing-weights.t: The mixing weights **π** are **0.30, 0.45 and 0.25**. They are positive and **add up to 1**: each is roughly the share of the data its component accounts for.

combine-components.t: At every spend value we add the three weighted curves: **π_A p_A(x) + π_B p_B(x) + π_C p_C(x)**. The thick curve is that sum.

overall-density.t: The sum is the **mixture density**: it rises at each clump and dips between them, like the data. At spend 3.5, in the valley, it is only **0.084**.

mixture-idea.t: A mixture builds a **complicated distribution from simple parts**. A, B and C are mathematical components, **not named customer types**, so they are tools for describing the data.
